ai-at-work.title: Pinterest launches an experimental AI shopping app called ‘Ask Pinterest’
ai-at-work.excerpt: Pinterest has launched 'Ask Pinterest,' an experimental AI-powered shopping app that lets users seek recommendations and inspiration through a conversational interface.
ai-at-work.dwp_take: Pinterest rolled out Ask Pinterest, an AI chatbot that lets users ask for shopping recommendations and inspiration instead of scrolling through pins. This matters because it signals how search behavior is shifting across platforms, and digital workplace teams are now figuring out how to optimize content for conversational AI rather than traditional keyword searches. Honestly, if Pinterest thinks people want to chat with an AI about throw pillows instead of endlessly scrolling, they're either brilliant or have fundamentally misunderstood why people use Pinterest in the first place.

ai-at-work.title: Ex-Cisco researchers launch Tenet Security to lock down rogue AI agents
ai-at-work.excerpt: Former Cisco artificial intelligence security researchers have launched a new company to tackle a problem that barely existed a year ago: securing the autonomous AI agents enterprises are handing the
ai-at-work.dwp_take: A group of ex-Cisco security researchers just launched Tenet Security to solve a brand new problem: stopping rogue AI agents from wrecking your enterprise systems before they go live. This matters because we're about to hand autonomous AI decision-making power over critical workflows, and nobody really knows how to stop them when they go sideways. Here's the thing though: we're building the parachute on the way down, which is how every major tech shift works, so at least someone experienced is finally paying attention.

ai-at-work.title: CYGNVS launches command center for crises caused by a company’s own AI
ai-at-work.excerpt: Cyber resilience company CYGNVS Inc. today launched its AI Incident Command Center, a platform built to help organizations manage operational crises caused by their own artificial intelligence deploym
ai-at-work.dwp_take: CYGNVS just launched a platform specifically designed to handle disasters caused by your own AI systems going haywire in production. This matters because as organizations rush to deploy AI across their operations, they're realizing nobody actually has a playbook for when these systems break, hallucinate, or cause compliance nightmares. Thirty years in this space taught me that we always build the safety net after someone falls off the tightrope, and this product is basically admitting we've already let the rope get pretty frayed.

ai-at-work.title: Databricks’ new agentic coworker Genie One brings AI automation to every part of the business
ai-at-work.excerpt: Big-data company Databricks Inc. is getting into the agentic artificial intelligence coworker game with the launch of a new tool called Genie One, aimed at helping business teams orchestrate workflows
ai-at-work.dwp_take: Databricks launched Genie One, an AI agent designed to automate workflows and orchestrate tasks across business operations, expanding beyond their earlier conversational analytics tool. Digital workplace pros need to pay attention because autonomous agents are moving from nice-to-have demos into actual work orchestration, which means your integration strategy and governance frameworks just got a lot more complicated. Look, everyone's bolting "agentic AI" onto their product roadmap these days, but the real question is whether Genie One actually reduces busywork or just creates a new layer of babysitting robots.

tools-tech.title: Here's a portable power bank that's actually worth its high price - especially if you travel
tools-tech.excerpt: The Cuktech 15 Air is a small yet energy-dense power bank that earns a ZDNET Lab Awards badge as the fastest-charging power bank we've tested.
tools-tech.dwp_take: ZDNet tested a portable power bank called the Cuktech 15 Air and found it charges faster than competitors while remaining compact enough to travel with. For remote workers and road warriors who live on video calls, a reliable power bank that actually delivers on speed matters because dead devices mean dead productivity. Look, I've seen people panic over a dying laptop during client calls for thirty years, so if this thing actually works, it's worth the price tag just for the peace of mind alone.

tools-tech.title: Malicious apps got into the Arch User Repository - how to protect yourself
tools-tech.excerpt: For the second time in a week, the AUR was found to contain malicious applications. What can Arch Linux users do about this?
tools-tech.dwp_take: Malicious apps slipped into the Arch User Repository twice in one week, giving bad actors a direct pipeline to developer machines and workstations. This matters because many tech teams run Arch or derivatives on their systems, and if your developers or IT staff got compromised through something they thought was legitimate, you've got a real problem on your hands. The AUR's openness is both its greatest strength and its Achilles heel, which means your people need to treat it like they treat sketchy USB drives at conferences: with healthy skepticism.

tools-tech.title: Microsoft launches Copilot Cowork with usage-based pricing
tools-tech.excerpt: Microsoft has introduced usage-based billing for Copilot Cowork, which is now generally available. Microsoft unveiled Copilot Cowork in March, pitching it as an AI agent that’s capable of independentl
tools-tech.dwp_take: Microsoft just rolled out pay-as-you-go pricing for Copilot Cowork, their AI agent that runs tasks independently even when your machine is sleeping. This matters because it finally gives organizations a way to test autonomous AI without committing to fixed costs, which could actually make adoption realistic instead of theoretical. The real question is whether teams will trust their valuable work to an AI agent running unsupervised, or if this just becomes another expensive experiment gathering dust in procurement.

tools-tech.title: Z.ai pitches GLM-5.2 for long-running software engineering tasks
tools-tech.excerpt: Z.ai has released GLM-5.2, an MIT-licensed open-source AI model designed for long-running software engineering tasks, as the Chinese company seeks to challenge proprietary coding models on cost and pe
tools-tech.dwp_take: Z.ai dropped GLM-5.2, an open-source AI model built for extended software engineering work that apparently competes with Claude and GPT-5 while being cheaper and MIT-licensed. This matters because it signals the coding AI space is finally getting real competition beyond the usual OpenAI and Anthropic duopoly, which could actually drive innovation instead of just higher bills. If a Chinese startup can match proprietary models at a fraction of the cost, enterprise development teams need to stop autopiloting toward whatever's loudest and actually evaluate what solves their problems.

digital-culture.title: Is technical literacy the new MBA?
digital-culture.excerpt: Traditional business degrees once guaranteed a path to leadership, but today’s market increasingly rewards technical literacy over classroom credentials. The shift reflects a fundamental change in how
digital-culture.dwp_take: Microsoft just published their quarterly earnings and half the analysis focused on AI productivity gains nobody can actually measure yet. The shift from "did you go to a good school" to "can you actually work in modern software systems" matters because it finally aligns hiring with reality instead of pedigree. Here's the thing though: technical literacy without judgment and communication skills is just expensive trouble waiting to happen, so let's not overcorrect and hire people who can code but can't explain why anyone should care.

digital-culture.title: Meta CTO Andrew Bosworth Admits the Company’s AI Reorg Was ‘Atrocious’
digital-culture.excerpt: In an internal memo seen by WIRED, Bosworth promised employees more stability, better communication, and the return of workplace perks as the company seeks to improve morale.
digital-culture.dwp_take: Meta's CTO admitted in an internal memo that his company botched a recent AI reorganization and is now promising employees stability, communication, and perks to fix morale. This matters because when a company of Meta's scale struggles with organizational chaos and employee trust, it signals that even tech giants can bungle change management, giving digital workplace leaders a cautionary tale worth studying. Here's the thing though: no amount of returned ping pong tables will fix the underlying problem that nobody actually told people what was happening during the reorganization in the first place.

Honestly, if your organization's security posture depends on employees NOT buying cheap routers from Prime Day deals, you've already lost the battle.

industry-news.title: Salesforce Makes $3.6B Play for AI Customer Service
industry-news.excerpt: Salesforce will buy Fin, formerly Intercom, for about $3.6 billion to expand Agentforce with AI customer service agents and support automation. The post Salesforce Makes $3.6B Play for AI Customer Ser
industry-news.dwp_take: Salesforce just dropped 3.6 billion dollars to buy Fin, the AI customer service platform formerly known as Intercom, to beef up its Agentforce offering with smarter automation and AI agents. This matters because every digital workplace is now figuring out how AI customer service fits into their employee tools and workflows, and Salesforce just signaled this is table stakes for enterprise platforms. Honestly, at that price tag Fin better not just be replacing helpful humans with chatbots that make customers angrier than they were before calling in.

industry-news.title: ShinyHunters Claims Council of Europe HR Data, Threatens Leak
industry-news.excerpt: ShinyHunters claims it stole 297GB of data from the Council of Europe, including payroll and medical records, but the organization has not confirmed a breach. The post ShinyHunters Claims Council of E
industry-news.dwp_take: A hacking group called ShinyHunters claims they've stolen nearly 300 gigabytes of HR data from the Council of Europe, including payroll and medical records, though the organization hasn't confirmed anything yet. This matters because if true, it's a textbook example of why your employee data governance and access controls need to be airtight, not aspirational. The Council of Europe dealing with this is like a fire safety inspector's house catching fire, except the fire might involve your entire workforce's personal information.

industry-news.title: Meta’s New Facebook ‘AI Mode’ Pulls From Groups, Reels, and Posts
industry-news.excerpt: Meta AI Mode brings AI-generated answers to Facebook search using public posts, raising questions about reliability and source visibility. The post Meta’s New Facebook ‘AI Mode’ Pulls From Groups, Ree
industry-news.dwp_take: Meta's rolling out an AI Mode on Facebook search that generates answers by pulling from public posts, groups, and reels without always showing where the information came from. For anyone managing internal communications or employee engagement platforms, this is a cautionary tale about what happens when you let AI summarize user-generated content without proper attribution or fact-checking. I give it six months before someone's relying on this for actual business decisions and wondering why their quarterly projections are based on a reel from 2019.
